yapese_yanolop.name: fashions with his mind the five further sky deities from whom the later gods descend
yapese_yanolop.notes: Created by the primordial sky-maker Gavur li yel yel from his hands and dirt, Yanolop in turn made five sky deities (four male and the female Matsugulop), among whose descendants is the sky high-god Yalafath.

sources.reference: Christian, The Caroline Islands (1899); Mitchell, Micronesian Mythology

zoroastrian_athwya.name: second mortal to press the haoma plant, earning as boon the birth of his son Thraetaona
zoroastrian_athwya.notes: In the Hom Yasht, Haoma names Athwya (Pers. Abtin) as the second man to prepare the sacred draught; his reward was the son Thraetaona/Fereydun who would bind the dragon Azhi Dahaka.

sources.reference: Hom Yasht, Yasna 9.7

zoroastrian_farangis.name: shields and spirits her infant son Kay Khosrow out of Turan to Iran after the murder of Siyavash
zoroastrian_farangis.notes: Daughter of Afrasiab of Turan and wife of Siyavash; after her husband's treacherous killing she hides their son, and when the hero Giv comes she flees with him and the boy across the river to Iran, securing the future ideal king.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Siyavash; Forud cycle)

zoroastrian_kay_kavus.name: builds an eagle-borne flying throne to assail heaven, and crashes from the sky
zoroastrian_kay_kavus.notes: In the Shahnameh the proud king lashes four meat-baited poles to his throne so that the eagles straining upward bear it aloft toward heaven; the eagles tire and he falls to earth, to be rescued by Rostam, the type-tale of his hubris.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Kay Kavus)

zoroastrian_rudaba.name: lets down her long black tresses from the tower as a rope for her lover Zal
zoroastrian_rudaba.notes: Princess of Kabul; in her courtship she loosens her hair down the tower wall for Zal to climb (he uses a lariat instead). Her labour with the giant child Rostam is so hard that Zal summons the Simorgh, by whose counsel the first caesarean birth is performed and she survives.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Zal and Rudaba; the birth of Rostam)

zoroastrian_sohrab.name: leads the Turanian host against Iran to find his father Rostam and is slain by him unrecognised
zoroastrian_sohrab.notes: Born to Rostam by Tahmineh of Samangan, the mighty youth marches on Iran hoping to find his father and place him on the throne; Afrasiab contrives that the two never know one another, and Rostam fatally wounds him in single combat, learning the truth only as he dies.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Rostam and Sohrab)

yanomami_yoasi.name: introduces death, sickness and misfortune into the well-ordered world
yanomami_yoasi.notes: Where his brother the demiurge Omama set the world in good order, the clumsy and harmful Yoasi acted wrongly and brought mortality and ills; the Yanomami die because of his doing rather than Omama's.

sources.reference: Kopenawa & Albert, The Falling Sky (2013)

yanomami_yoawe.name: with his twin wins water and cultivated plants and teaches the people the arts of living
yanomami_yoawe.notes: Twin culture-hero and brother of Omawe; together they obtain water and cultivated plants from the daughter of the water-being and instruct the Yanomami, including how to raise the communal house.

sources.reference: Kopenawa & Albert, The Falling Sky (2013); Wilbert & Simoneau, Folk Literature of the Yanomami Indians

zoroastrian_mithra.name: golden weapons - spear, bow and a thousand arrows

sources.reference: Mihr Yasht (Yasht 10), the arming of Mithra

zoroastrian_mithra.name: chariot drawn by four white immortal horses

sources.reference: Mihr Yasht (Yasht 10)

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Kay Khosrow)

sources.reference: Marcus & Flannery, Zapotec Civilization (1996); Cordova, Vocabulario en lengua zapoteca (1578)

zoroastrian_keresaspa.gloss: of manly mind / brave-minded (standing Avestan epithet of Keresaspa)

sources.reference: Yasht 19 (Zamyad Yasht); Yasna 9 (Hom Yasht)
Aban Yasht (Yasht 5.34); Hom Yasht (Yasna 9.8)

zoroastrian_ahura_mazda.name: the day Ohrmazd (first day of every month) and the feast-days bearing the divine name
zoroastrian_ahura_mazda.cadence: the first day of each of the twelve months; and Day Ohrmazd of Month Dadv (Frawardigan season)
zoroastrian_ahura_mazda.notes: In the Zoroastrian 365-day calendar the first day of every month is dedicated to Ahura Mazda (Ohrmazd), kept with the Hormazd Niyayesh; the coincidence of name-day and name-month (jashan) is specially observed.

sources.reference: Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism; Zoroastrian religious calendar (Avesta.org)

zoroastrian_asha_vahishta.name: the day Ardwahisht and tending of the sacred fire
zoroastrian_asha_vahishta.cadence: the third day of every month and the second month, with name-day jashan
zoroastrian_asha_vahishta.notes: As Amesha Spenta of Best Truth and guardian of fire, Asha Vahishta (Ardwahisht) is honoured on his calendar day and month and in the care and consecration of the temple flame.

sources.reference: Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism; Zoroastrian religious calendar (Avesta.org)

zoroastrian_khshathra_vairya.name: the day Shahrewar and offerings on behalf of metals
zoroastrian_khshathra_vairya.cadence: the fourth day of every month and the sixth month
zoroastrian_khshathra_vairya.notes: Amesha Spenta of Dominion and guardian of metals, honoured on his named day and month; in observance metal objects are an emblem of his protection.

sources.reference: Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism; Zoroastrian religious calendar (Avesta.org)

zoroastrian_haurvatat.name: the day Khordad and the consecration of the waters
zoroastrian_haurvatat.cadence: the sixth day of every month and the third month
zoroastrian_haurvatat.notes: Amesha Spenta of Wholeness/Health and guardian of the waters; honoured on her named day and month, paired with her sister Ameretat (Amurdad).

sources.reference: Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism; Zoroastrian religious calendar (Avesta.org)

zoroastrian_ameretat.name: the day Amurdad and the offering of plants
zoroastrian_ameretat.cadence: the seventh day of every month and the fifth month
zoroastrian_ameretat.notes: Amesha Spenta of Immortality and guardian of plants; honoured on her named day and month, paired with her sister Haurvatat (Khordad).

sources.reference: Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism; Zoroastrian religious calendar (Avesta.org)

zoroastrian_mithra.name: Mehregan, the autumn feast of Mithra
zoroastrian_mithra.cadence: annually, day Mihr of month Mihr (the seventh month)
zoroastrian_mithra.notes: Great autumn festival on the name-day-in-name-month of Mithra; one of the two pillar feasts of the Iranian year with Nowruz. In Yazd villages a sheep was sacrificed for Mihr on Mehregan and the three following days, the fat cast on the temple fire.

sources.reference: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Mehragan'; Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism

zoroastrian_aredvi_sura_anahita.name: Abanagan, the feast of the Waters, and her temple cult
zoroastrian_aredvi_sura_anahita.cadence: annually, day Aban of month Aban (the eighth month, ~26 October)
zoroastrian_aredvi_sura_anahita.notes: Feast of the waters dedicated to Aredvi Sura Anahita, kept at rivers and springs. Uniquely among Iranian deities she received an image-cult: Artaxerxes II set up statues of her in the chief cities and her great temple stood at Istakhr.

sources.reference: Aban Yasht (Yasht 5)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Anahid ii. The Cult and its Diffusion'; Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism

zoroastrian_atar.name: the day Adar and the perpetual fire of the fire-temples
zoroastrian_atar.cadence: the ninth day of every month and the ninth month, with the feast Adargan
zoroastrian_atar.notes: Fire as the visible presence of Asha is tended unceasingly in the fire-temples, the highest grade being the Atash Bahram ('Victorious Fire'); the yazata Atar is specially honoured on his name-day and month (Adargan).

sources.reference: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Atas'; Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism

zoroastrian_haoma.name: the Yasna haoma-pressing rite
zoroastrian_haoma.cadence: in every performance of the Yasna liturgy
zoroastrian_haoma.notes: The yazata is worshipped through the act central to his being: the priestly pounding of the haoma twigs with water in the mortar during the Yasna, the pressed draught then offered and consumed. The Hom Yasht is recited in his praise.

sources.reference: Hom Yasht, Yasna 9-11

zapotec_cocijo.name: rain-petition and bloodletting offerings to the lightning-god
zapotec_cocijo.cadence: at planting and corn-harvest and in time of drought
zapotec_cocijo.notes: As the bringer of rain Cocijo was the foremost recipient of Zapotec offering: copal incense, sacrificed birds and small animals, autosacrificial blood drawn by priests from beneath the tongue and behind the ear and caught on feathers, and, to obtain rain, human sacrifice chiefly of children.

sources.reference: Marcus & Flannery, Zapotec Civilization (1996); Whitecotton, The Zapotecs (1977)

zapotec_pitao_bezelao.name: mortuary offerings to the lord of the dead at Mitla
zapotec_pitao_bezelao.notes: Bezelao, chief god of death and patron of Mitla (Lyobaa, 'place of rest'), received funerary offerings and the petitions of the sick; Mitla was the great oracular necropolis and seat of the high priest (Uija-tao).

sources.reference: Marcus & Flannery, Zapotec Civilization (1996); Whitecotton, The Zapotecs (1977)

zapotec_pitao_cozobi.name: first-fruits and harvest offerings of maize
zapotec_pitao_cozobi.cadence: at the maize harvest and sowing
zapotec_pitao_cozobi.notes: The maize-god received offerings of grain, copal and blood tied to the agricultural round, the harvest and corn-fertility rites at which the colaní (diviner) and priesthood officiated.

sources.reference: Marcus & Flannery, Zapotec Civilization (1996)

yemoja.name: Yemoja Gelede-Efe festival at Abeokuta and procession to the River Ogun
yemoja.cadence: annually/biennially in Ogun State (Ibara quarter, Abeokuta)
yemoja.notes: Her principal Yorubaland shrine is at Abeokuta, where the Ibara people coordinate the worship of the river Odo-Ogun; the Yemoja festival brings processions to the river with music, dance, prayers and offerings, kin to the Osun-Osogbo rites.

sources.reference: Bascom, The Yoruba of Southwestern Nigeria (1969)
Drewal & Drewal, Gelede: Art and Female Power among the Yoruba

sacredAnimals.name: the four white horses of his chariot
sacredAnimals.notes: Mithra drives a chariot drawn by four immortal white horses of one colour, emblems of light and purity in the Mihr Yasht.

sources.reference: Mihr Yasht (Yasht 10)

attributes.name: the ever-burning Atash Bahram
attributes.notes: Atar is manifest as the consecrated perpetual flame of the fire-temple, the highest grade the Atash Bahram or 'Victorious Fire'; it is never imaged anthropomorphically but tended as the visible presence of Asha.

sources.reference: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Atas'; Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism

attributes.name: the hero's heavy club/mace
attributes.notes: The Sama hero Keresaspa (Pers. Garshasp) is defined by his great club, the gada-bearing strong-man who slays the horned dragon and the demon Gandarewa.

sources.reference: Zamyad Yasht (Yasht 19); Ferdowsi/Asadi, Garshasp-nama

attributes.name: serpents springing from the shoulders (Zahhak)
attributes.notes: In the Shahnameh the dragon, incarnate as the tyrant Zahhak, has two black serpents growing from his shoulders that must be fed daily on human brains, the visual signature of the Lie-king.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Zahhak)

attributes.name: water-jar and lightning-bolts
attributes.notes: On the Lambityeco stucco busts Cocijo holds a jar spilling water in one hand and bolts of lightning in the other; his brows render the heavens, his lower lids the clouds, and his forked serpent-tongue the lightning.

sources.reference: Caso & Bernal, Urnas de Oaxaca (1952); Sellen, El cielo compartido (2007)

attributes.name: the four directional Cocijos
attributes.notes: Cocijo is quartered to the cardinal directions: the four 65-day divisions of the 260-day ritual calendar were themselves called cocijos, implying a distinct Cocijo and colour for each quarter of the world.

sources.reference: Marcus & Flannery, Zapotec Civilization (1996)

sacredAnimals.name: the albatross mui-bab
sacredAnimals.notes: The sky high-god's messenger is the albatross (mui-bab), and he was sometimes thought to be incarnate in it; the souls of the dead go to his home Falraman.

sources.reference: Mitchell, Micronesian Mythology; Oxford Reference, 'Yalafath'

attributes.name: the bark-and-hide kína mask of the Moon-woman
attributes.notes: In the kína (Yámana men's ceremony) Hánuxa is impersonated by a conical mask of bark sewn with whale-gut and painted; the colours of the kína masks signified the skies (red, white, black).

sources.reference: Gusinde, Die Feuerland-Indianer II: Die Yamana (1937)
Wilbert, Folk Literature of the Yamana Indians (1977)

attributes.name: the masked, painted body of the spirit who rises through the fire
attributes.notes: Yetaita, the dread spirit of the kína lodge, is shown as a masked figure painted in the directional black/red/white of the ceremony who terrifies the male novices by emerging from beneath the earth up through the fire.

sources.reference: Gusinde, Die Feuerland-Indianer II: Die Yamana (1937)

attributes.name: luminous beings small as shining dust, dancing on sky-mirrors
attributes.notes: The xapiri appear as humanlike beings tiny as particles of shining dust who descend dancing upon great mirrors that come down from the sky, brilliant and beautiful as they come to the shaman who has drunk yãkoana.

sources.reference: Kopenawa & Albert, The Falling Sky (2013)

attributes.name: urucum paint and bright feather regalia
attributes.notes: Their bodies are painted red with urucum (annatto) and drawn over with black; their heads bear the white down/feathers of the king vulture and their arm-bands the feathers of macaw, parrot and cujubim, their waists wrapped with toucan tails.

sources.reference: Kopenawa & Albert, The Falling Sky (2013)
